t: How To Drench Your Students In Learning
q: One of the biggest mistakes teachers make is that they get too involved in student work.
In fact, once your students become absorbed in independent or group work, once they’re doing as you ask, it’s best to observe from a distance.
When your students are on task and engaged in the work you’ve given them, it’s a sign that deep learning is taking place.
One of the goals of effective teaching is to continually extend the amount of time your students work independently and without your input.
It means that you’ll take note of their strengths, weaknesses, and struggles in order to inform future instruction.
Set your students up for success, then step off the stage . Recede into the shadows.
x: Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Extending independent work time without teacher interference builds grit, perseverance, and concentration.
Stepping back doesn't mean disengaging — teachers should observe closely to inform future instruction.
The teacher's job is to model and inspire, then step off the stage and let students take ownership of learning.

t: How To Speak So Students Listen
q: If you cut the amount of talking you do by a third, and focus only on what your students need to know, then what you say will have greater impact.
When you lower your voice, however, and speak just loud enough for students in the back of the room to hear, they instinctively lean in. They stop moving and rustling.
When you repeat the same directions over and over, you train your students not to listen to you the first time. You encourage apathy and lighten their load of responsibility.
Because your students have grown accustomed to you taking on the burden for their listening, they may very well ignore you.
They’ll begin looking at you, tracking your movements, and anticipating what you want them to do next.
They’ll become empowered to do for themselves because responsibility feels good. It’s important. It fills with pride.
x: Teachers who talk less give their words greater impact and make them easier for students to tune into.
Lowering your voice, rather than raising it, causes students to instinctively lean in and pay closer attention.
Repeating directions trains students not to listen the first time; saying it once creates urgency.
Over time, students who take ownership of listening become more engaged, attentive, and self-directed.

Over time, students begin tracking the teacher's movements, anticipating directions, and taking pride in completing tasks independently — outcomes Linsin frames as evidence that responsibility has shifted appropriately…
Linsin identifies how a teacher speaks — not just what they say — as a decisive factor in classroom listening.

t: Why Gentleness Is A Strong Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: There is a common misconception that you must have a big presence to be an effective leader.

21st-century students respond best to a calm, even-handed approach to classroom management. They appreciate honesty and kindness. They respect it, and thus, are quick to listen and please their teacher.
Without saying a word, a gentle presence removes classroom stress, tension, and anxiety. It soothes and alleviates excitability and distraction—which are two major causes of misbehavior.
Enforcing consequences calmly and consistently diminishes the possibility that your students will argue, complain, or lie to you about their misbehavior.
Weakness is when you lose emotional control. It’s when you lecture, berate, and admonish students instead of following your classroom management plan .
Martin Luther King Jr. was gentle. So were Rosa Parks and Abraham Lincoln. And so are the happiest and most effective teachers on Earth.
x: Linsin challenges the notion that effective classroom leadership requires a big, forceful presence, arguing instead that gentleness — not weakness — is the true hallmark of influential teachers.
Gentleness, not forcefulness, is what 21st-century students respect and respond to as classroom leadership.
A gentle presence reduces classroom stress, tension, and anxiety without a word being spoken.
Enforcing consequences calmly diminishes arguing, complaining, and pushback from students.
Gentleness is distinct from weakness; weakness is losing emotional control, while gentleness signals calm confidence.

Linsin invokes historical figures known for their calm strength — Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, and Abraham Lincoln — to reinforce that gentleness and strength are not opposites but complements.

t: An Easy Way To Keep Your Cool When Students Misbehave nts-misbehave/
q: The advice is this: When enforcing consequences, think like a referee.
A referee’s job is to make sure players abide by the agreed-upon rules of the game. That’s it. They make no judgments or decisions of their own accord.
A good referee is defined by their calm and consistent adherence to the rule book—the purpose of which is to make the game safe and fair for all participants.
Teachers who are inconsistent and enforce consequences based on how the misbehavior makes them feel, who is doing the misbehaving, or the perceived severity of the misbehavior also lose control.
As soon as a student strays from your rule book ( classroom management plan ), follow through like a referee in the Super Bowl.
Because when you focus on being a good referee, not only will you have excellent control of your class, but keeping your cool will be easy.
x: Revisiting reader-favorite advice, Linsin offers a simple mental model for staying calm while enforcing consequences: think like a referee.
A good referee follows a fixed rule book consistently, which keeps a game (or classroom) fair and under control.
A good referee follows a fixed rule book consistently, which keeps a game (or classroom) fair and under control.

Applying the analogy directly to teaching, Linsin argues that teachers who base consequences on mood, favoritism, or perceived severity — rather than on a fixed classroom management plan — similarly lose control…

t: How To Ask Your Students For The Moon . . . And Get It d-get-it/
q: I’ve since learned that as long as you create a classroom your students look forward to, you can’t ask for too much. You can’t have expectations that are too high.
Your students will rise to meet your high bar as long as they know you care enough to make it worth their while.
As long as you make your classroom an experience they enjoy being part of—better yet, love being part of—they will follow you to the ends of the earth.
He never mentioned the lengthy independent work periods, the demand for flawless routines, or my neverending calls for excellence.
Because when a spirit of fun and humor are part of the fabric of your classroom, you can ask for more and for better every day of the week.
x: Students who experience a classroom as genuinely enjoyable will look back fondly on hard work and high expectations rather than resent them.
As long as students feel a class is worth their while, they will follow a teacher's high expectations willingly.
Rigorous work habits and demanding routines can coexist with — and even be remembered as part of — a beloved classroom experience.
The former student recalls the hard work, the challenging routines, and the neverending calls for excellence not as burdens but as cherished memories tied to fun, friendship, and connection.
A spirit of fun and humor in the classroom fabric enables teachers to ask more of students without pushback.
